lead: A deadlock occurs when a group of processes each wait for a resource that another member of the group holds. The operating system models the situation with processes, resources, and allocation matrices. By checking the model we can see why deadlocks happen and what conditions must be true for them to exist. The model is used in exam questions, in OS design, and in real systems such as database lock managers or UPI transaction handling.
prereq: You need: understanding of processes and resources from Monitors for synchronization and of mutexes from Mutex locks and semaphores.

blocks.text: The model has a set of processes P = {P1, P2, …, Pm} and a set of resource types R = {R1, R2, …, Rn}. Each resource type Rj has Ej identical instances. The total number of instances is a vector E = (E1, E2, …, En).

Two matrices describe the current state. The allocation matrix A has entry Aij = number of instances of Rj held by Pi. The request matrix Q has entry Qij = number of instances of Rj that Pi still needs to complete.

blocks.where: For each resource type Rj, the sum of allocated instances and free instances equals the total instances Ej.

blocks.text: Fj = number of free (unallocated) instances of resource Rj. Since free instances plus allocated instances equal the total instances, the equality ∑i Aij + Fj = Ej always holds.
A snapshot of A and Q together forms the resource‑allocation graph. Nodes represent processes and resources. An edge Pi → Rj means Pi is requesting Rj. An edge Rj → Pi means Rj is allocated to Pi.

items: Processes are active entities that execute code.
Resources are physical or logical items such as CPU cores, memory pages, or database locks.
Allocation matrix shows who owns what now.
Request matrix shows what each process still needs.

sections.h3: Four necessary conditions for a deadlock

blocks.text: A deadlock can exist only if all four conditions hold simultaneously. If any one condition is broken, the deadlock cannot persist.

items: Mutual exclusion – at most one process can use a resource instance at a time.
Hold and wait – a process holds at least one resource while waiting for another.
No preemption – a resource cannot be forcibly taken away from a process; it must be released voluntarily.
Circular wait – there exists a circular chain of processes Pi1 → Pi2 → … → Pik → Pi1 such that each process Pi holds at least one resource needed by the next process in the chain.

blocks.text: To verify a deadlock in a snapshot:

items: Step 1: Identify the resources each process currently holds (allocation matrix).
Step 2: Identify the resources each process still needs (request matrix).
Step 3: Check the four conditions in the current snapshot.
Step 4: If all are true, the system is in a deadlocked state.
Step 5: The deadlock conclusion is as above.

blocks.text: In many textbooks this set of conditions is called the “deadlock conditions” or “deadlock characterization”. The model helps designers decide which condition to break in order to prevent deadlocks.
The next chapter describes how to break one of the four conditions on purpose. Those techniques are called deadlock prevention and are covered in Methods for handling deadlocks; deadlock prevention.

examples.question: Two database transactions T_A and T_B need exclusive locks on rows X and Y. T_A currently holds lock X and now requests lock Y. T_B holds lock Y and now requests lock X. Draw the resource‑allocation graph, list the four necessary conditions, and state whether a deadlock exists.
steps: Step 1: Identify processes: P1 = T_A, P2 = T_B.
Step 2: Identify resources: R1 = lock on X, R2 = lock on Y.
Step 3: Build the graph: P1 → R2 (request), R2 → P2 (allocation), P2 → R1 (request), R1 → P1 (allocation).
• Mutual exclusion – a lock can be held by only one transaction. True.
• Hold and wait – each transaction holds one lock while waiting for the other. True.
• No preemption – locks are not taken away forcefully. True.
• Circular wait – P1 waits for R2 held by P2, and P2 waits for R1 held by P1. True.
Step 5: All four conditions hold, so the system is deadlocked.
examples.answer: The system is in deadlock because all four necessary conditions are satisfied.

traps: Confusing “no preemption” with “preemptive scheduling”. The condition is about resources, not CPU time slices.
Assuming that breaking any one condition automatically resolves every deadlock. In practice the system must enforce the break at the right time.
Missing the circular‑wait condition when the graph has a hidden cycle of length three or more.

quiz.q: What is the name of the condition that requires a resource to be used by only one process at a time?
Explain why the “hold and wait” condition contributes to deadlock formation.
quiz.a: A process that already holds a resource may request another one. If the second resource is held by another waiting process, both block each other, creating a deadlock.

quiz.q: Given two processes P1, P2 and two resources R1, R2 with allocation matrix A = [[1,0],[0,1]] and request matrix Q = [[0,1],[1,0]], determine whether a deadlock exists.
quiz.a: All four conditions hold, so a deadlock exists.

quiz.q: A system has three identical printers (R1). Process P1 holds one printer and requests another. Process P2 holds one printer and requests none. Process P3 holds none and requests one printer. Is the system deadlocked?
quiz.a: No deadlock. There are free printer instances; the request of P1 can be satisfied.

quiz.q: In a banking transaction system, each transaction needs locks on two accounts. Describe how breaking the circular‑wait condition can be enforced.
quiz.a: Impose a total ordering on account numbers and require every transaction to request locks in increasing order. This prevents cycles.

quiz.q: A resource‑allocation graph shows a cycle involving three processes and three resources. List the four necessary conditions and indicate which one could be removed to eliminate the deadlock.
quiz.a: Mutual exclusion, hold‑and‑wait, no‑preemption, circular‑wait. Removing circular‑wait (by ordering resources) breaks the deadlock.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, deadlock analysis is used in database concurrency control, distributed transaction managers, and cloud resource schedulers. Research explores dynamic detection algorithms that run with low overhead on large clusters. New curricula add formal verification tools such as model checkers to prove absence of deadlock in concurrent code. Students interested in this area can search for “resource allocation graph deadlock detection” and “formal methods for concurrency”.
